# Resumable Checkout for Credit Packs

> Two UX patterns for letting users resume abandoned or partial credit pack purchases without creating duplicate Payment Intents

## The Use Case

Your app sells credit packs — fixed bundles of platform credits at set prices:

<Frame>
  <img src="/_mintlify/image/unifold/images/credit-packs-example.png" alt="Example credit pack purchase UI showing four packs: 5,000 credits for $5, 11,000 credits for $9.99, 30,000 credits for $24.99, and 65,000 credits for $49.99" />
</Frame>

Each purchase creates a [Payment Intent](/developer/checkout/overview) and opens a checkout modal. But users abandon checkouts — they close the modal, their browser crashes, or they get distracted. Without a resumption strategy, you end up creating duplicate Payment Intents every time they click "Buy Now" again.

This recipe presents **two UX patterns** for handling this. Choose the one that fits your product.

<Info>
  This recipe is specifically designed for **credit pack purchases** — fungible, fixed-price bundles with no inventory or shipping concerns. Product-based checkout (variable carts, stock management, etc.) requires different patterns.
</Info>

***

## Pattern A: Inline Resume on the Pack Grid

Modify the pack cards themselves to reflect pending payment state. When a user has an unfinished purchase for a pack, the "Buy Now" button becomes "Continue Payment" — right where they'd normally buy.

**What the user sees when they have a pending \$9.99 purchase:**

<Frame caption="The 11,000 Credits pack shows a partial payment warning with Continue and Cancel actions instead of Buy Now">
  <img src="/_mintlify/image/unifold/images/inline-resume-pack-grid-example.png" alt="Pack grid where the 11,000 Credits card shows a Partial Payment warning with Continue and Cancel buttons, while other packs show the normal Buy Now button" />
</Frame>

### How it works

When the user clicks "Buy Now" on a pack, your backend queries the Unifold API on the fly to check whether that user already has an incomplete Payment Intent for that pack — and either resumes it or creates a new one.

The key: when you create a Payment Intent, store the `pack_id` in `metadata` so you can match it back later.

**At creation time:**

<CodeGroup>
  ```typescript Node theme={null}
  const pi = await unifold.paymentIntents.create({
    amount: pack.amountSmallestUnit,
    currency: "usdc",
    destination_network: "base",
    recipient_address: recipientAddress,
    external_user_id: authenticatedUserId,
    description: `${pack.credits.toLocaleString()} Credits Pack`,
    metadata: { pack_id: pack.id, credits: String(pack.credits) },
    settlement_tolerance_percent: 1,
  });
  ```

  ```bash curl theme={null}
  curl -X POST https://api.unifold.io/v1/payment_intents \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_..." \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
      "amount": "9990000",
      "currency": "usdc",
      "destination_network": "base",
      "recipient_address": "0x742d35Cc6634C0532925a3b844Bc9e7595f0aB12",
      "external_user_id": "user_abc",
      "description": "11,000 Credits Pack",
      "metadata": { "pack_id": "pack_11k", "credits": "11000" },
      "settlement_tolerance_percent": 1
    }'
  ```
</CodeGroup>

**At click time — check before creating:**

When the user clicks a pack, your backend fetches their pending Payment Intents, finds any that match the clicked pack (via `metadata`, `description`, or whichever field you use to identify packs), and decides to resume or create:

```typescript theme={null}
async function handleBuyPack(authenticatedUserId: string, pack: Pack) {
  const pending = await unifold.paymentIntents.list({
    external_user_id: authenticatedUserId,
    status: ["requires_payment", "processing"],
  });

  const existingForPack = pending.data.find(
    (pi) => pi.metadata?.pack_id === pack.id
  );

  if (existingForPack) {
    switch (existingForPack.status) {
      case "processing":
        return { action: "wait" as const };
      case "requires_payment":
        return {
          action: "resume" as const,
          clientSecret: existingForPack.client_secret,
        };
    }
  }

  const pi = await unifold.paymentIntents.create({
    amount: pack.amountSmallestUnit,
    currency: "usdc",
    destination_network: "base",
    recipient_address: recipientAddress,
    external_user_id: authenticatedUserId,
    description: `${pack.credits.toLocaleString()} Credits Pack`,
    metadata: { pack_id: pack.id, credits: String(pack.credits) },
    settlement_tolerance_percent: 1,
  });

  return { action: "checkout" as const, clientSecret: pi.client_secret };
}
```

The frontend handles the response:

```typescript theme={null}
const { beginCheckout } = useUnifold();

async function onBuyNowClick(pack: Pack) {
  const result = await api.handleBuyPack(pack.id);

  switch (result.action) {
    case "checkout":
    case "resume":
      await beginCheckout({ clientSecret: result.clientSecret });
      break;
    case "wait":
      showProcessingMessage();
      break;
  }
}
```

From the user's perspective, clicking "Buy Now" on a pack they previously abandoned **just works** — the checkout modal reopens where they left off. They never know a previous Payment Intent existed. If the payment is already processing, they see a reassurance message instead of accidentally creating a duplicate.

<Info>
  The user always clicks the same "Buy Now" button. The resume logic is invisible — your backend handles it behind the scenes by querying the Payment Intent API at click time. No "Continue Payment" button is needed unless you want to show pending state on the pack grid proactively (see "Optional: showing pending state on the grid" below).
</Info>

### Optional: showing pending state on the grid

If you want the pack grid to reflect pending state *before* the user clicks, fetch pending Payment Intents when the grid loads and match them to packs:

```typescript theme={null}
async function getPackStates(authenticatedUserId: string, packs: Pack[]) {
  const pending = await unifold.paymentIntents.list({
    external_user_id: authenticatedUserId,
    status: ["requires_payment", "processing"],
  });

  return packs.map((pack) => {
    const pi = pending.data.find((p) => p.metadata?.pack_id === pack.id);

    if (!pi) return { pack, uiState: "available" as const };

    if (pi.status === "processing") {
      const received = parseInt(pi.amount_received);
      return {
        pack,
        uiState: received > 0 ? "partially_paid" as const : "processing" as const,
        clientSecret: pi.client_secret,
        amountReceived: pi.amount_received_usd,
      };
    }

    return {
      pack,
      uiState: "requires_payment" as const,
      clientSecret: pi.client_secret,
    };
  });
}
```

This turns the grid into the version shown above — packs with pending payments show "Continue" instead of "Buy Now." But this is optional; the click-time check alone is enough to prevent duplicates and enable resumption.

### When to choose this pattern

| Strength                                                 | Limitation                                                   |
| -------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Seamless — the user clicks "Buy Now" and it just resumes | One API call per click to check for existing Payment Intents |
| Payment Intent API is the source of truth                | Optional grid-level state adds a list call on page load      |
| Resume is invisible to the user — same button, same flow |                                                              |
| Prevents accidental duplicates by design                 |                                                              |

<Tip>
  This is the better pattern if the pack grid is the primary (or only) place users interact with purchases. The recovery is invisible — it just works when they come back.
</Tip>

***

## Pattern B: Pending Payments List

Show a dedicated "Pending Payments" section that lists all incomplete Payment Intents for the authenticated user. Each row has its own "Resume" button. The pack grid stays unchanged — always showing "Buy Now."

**What the user sees:**

<Frame caption="A Pending Payments section above the pack grid, listing incomplete purchases with Resume and Cancel actions">
  <img src="/_mintlify/image/unifold/images/pending-payments-list-example.png" alt="UI mockup showing a Pending Payments section with two items — an 11,000 Credits payment started 2 hours ago and a 30,000 Credits payment processing for 5 minutes — above a Buy Extra Credit grid with four pack options" />
</Frame>

### How it works

Your backend queries the Unifold API on the fly once the user is authenticated against your auth system.

The flow is:

1. User logs in → your backend knows their `external_user_id`
2. Backend calls the [List Payment Intents API](/api-reference/payment-intents/list), filtering by that user and `processing` status
3. Each returned Payment Intent carries `metadata`, `description`, `client_secret`, and payment progress — everything you need to render the list and match each one back to a pack

We recommend filtering by **`processing` only** — these are payments where funds have already been received and the user needs to see them. Since Payment Intents remain open indefinitely until paid or [canceled](/api-reference/payment-intents/cancel), including `requires_payment` can show a long list of stale, unfulfilled intents that the user never canceled.

<CodeGroup>
  ```typescript Node theme={null}
  const processingIntents = await unifold.paymentIntents.list({
    external_user_id: authenticatedUserId,
    status: ["processing"],
  });
  ```

  ```bash curl theme={null}
  curl "https://api.unifold.io/v1/payment_intents?external_user_id=user_abc&status=processing" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_..."
  ```
</CodeGroup>

If you prefer to also show `requires_payment` intents (so users can resume abandoned payments they never paid into), add it to the filter:

<CodeGroup>
  ```typescript Node theme={null}
  const incompleteIntents = await unifold.paymentIntents.list({
    external_user_id: authenticatedUserId,
    status: ["requires_payment", "processing"],
  });
  ```

  ```bash curl theme={null}
  curl "https://api.unifold.io/v1/payment_intents?external_user_id=user_abc&status=requires_payment&status=processing" \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_..."
  ```
</CodeGroup>

<Note>
  If you include `requires_payment`, consider periodically [canceling stale ones](/api-reference/payment-intents/cancel) so the list doesn't grow indefinitely.
</Note>

### Tying Payment Intents back to packs

Each Payment Intent needs to carry enough information to identify which pack it belongs to. You set this at creation time using `metadata` and/or `description`:

<CodeGroup>
  ```typescript Node theme={null}
  const pi = await unifold.paymentIntents.create({
    amount: "9990000",
    currency: "usdc",
    destination_network: "base",
    recipient_address: recipientAddress,
    external_user_id: authenticatedUserId,
    description: "11,000 Credits Pack",
    metadata: { pack_id: "pack_11k", credits: "11000" },
    settlement_tolerance_percent: 1,
  });
  ```

  ```bash curl theme={null}
  curl -X POST https://api.unifold.io/v1/payment_intents \
    -H "Authorization: Bearer sk_live_..." \
    -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
    -d '{
      "amount": "9990000",
      "currency": "usdc",
      "destination_network": "base",
      "recipient_address": "0x742d35Cc6634C0532925a3b844Bc9e7595f0aB12",
      "external_user_id": "user_abc",
      "description": "11,000 Credits Pack",
      "metadata": { "pack_id": "pack_11k", "credits": "11000" },
      "settlement_tolerance_percent": 1
    }'
  ```
</CodeGroup>

When you list pending Payment Intents later, you match them back:

```typescript theme={null}
function resolvePackFromIntent(pi: PaymentIntent, packs: Pack[]): Pack | null {
  // Option 1: Match on metadata (structured, recommended)
  if (pi.metadata?.pack_id) {
    return packs.find((p) => p.id === pi.metadata.pack_id) ?? null;
  }

  // Option 2: Match on description (human-readable fallback)
  if (pi.description) {
    return packs.find((p) => pi.description?.includes(p.name)) ?? null;
  }

  return null;
}
```

<Note>
  We recommend `metadata` for matching — it's structured and won't break if you rename a pack. But if you already have a convention using `description` or `amount` to identify products, that works too. The goal is simply to tie each Payment Intent back to the right pack using whatever field your system already relies on.
</Note>

### Rendering the list

With the Payment Intent data and pack matching in place, the frontend is straightforward:

```typescript theme={null}
function PendingPaymentsList({ intents, packs }: Props) {
  const { beginCheckout } = useUnifold();

  return intents.map((pi) => {
    const pack = resolvePackFromIntent(pi, packs);
    const canResume = pi.status === "requires_payment";
    const isProcessing = pi.status === "processing";
    const received = parseInt(pi.amount_received);
    const total = parseInt(pi.amount);

    return (
      <div key={pi.id}>
        <span>{pack?.name ?? pi.description} ({formatUsd(pi.amount_usd)})</span>

        {isProcessing && received > 0 && (
          <span>Paid: {formatUsd(pi.amount_received_usd)} · Remaining: {formatUsd(total - received)}</span>
        )}

        <span>{isProcessing ? "Processing..." : "Payment started"}</span>

        {canResume && (
          <>
            <button onClick={() => beginCheckout({ clientSecret: pi.client_secret })}>
              Resume
            </button>
            <button onClick={() => cancelPaymentIntent(pi.id)}>
              Cancel
            </button>
          </>
        )}
        {isProcessing && (
          <button onClick={() => refreshStatus(pi.id)}>
            Refresh status
          </button>
        )}
      </div>
    );
  });
}
```

### Preventing duplicates

Since the pack grid always shows "Buy Now," you should still guard against creating duplicate Payment Intents when the user clicks "Buy Now" on a pack that already has a pending payment. This is the same check-before-create pattern used in Pattern A — query the Payment Intent API and match on `metadata`, `description`, or whichever field identifies the pack before calling `create`.

### When to choose this pattern

| Strength                                             | Limitation                                                       |
| ---------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Payment Intent API is the source of truth            | Users must notice the pending payments section                   |
| Shows all pending payments at once in a single list  | Pack grid doesn't reflect pending state (always shows "Buy Now") |
| Simple to implement — query on the fly after auth    | Adds an API call per page load (cacheable)                       |
| Works well as a standalone "My Payments" page        |                                                                  |
| Duplicate guard is just a list query before creation |                                                                  |

<Tip>
  This is the better pattern if you already have an account/billing section where users expect to manage payments, or if you want all incomplete purchases visible in one list.
</Tip>

***

## Combining Both Patterns

For the best experience, use both patterns together. Each serves a different purpose:

* **Pattern A (pack grid)** handles the click-time check — when the user clicks "Buy Now," your backend queries for `requires_payment` and `processing` intents for that specific pack to decide whether to resume or create. This prevents duplicates and makes resume invisible.
* **Pattern B (list)** surfaces `processing` intents — payments where funds have already been received. Show these in a dedicated section so the user knows money is in flight, even if they navigate away from the pack grid.

We recommend Pattern B only list `processing` intents, since `requires_payment` intents haven't received any funds and the list can grow with every abandoned checkout. But this is your call — if you want to give users visibility into all incomplete purchases so they can manually cancel stale ones, including `requires_payment` in the list is a valid pattern too.

```mermaid theme={null}
flowchart TD
    A[User opens credit store] --> B[List processing Payment Intents for user]
    B --> C{Any processing intents?}
    C -->|Yes| D[Show Processing Payments section + pack grid]
    C -->|No| E[Show normal pack grid only]
    
    D --> F[User clicks Continue on processing payment]
    F --> G[beginCheckout with existing client_secret]
    
    D --> H[User clicks Buy Now on a pack]
    E --> H
    H --> I[Backend checks for existing intent for this pack]
    I -->|requires_payment found| G
    I -->|processing found| J[Show processing message]
    I -->|No existing| K[Create new Payment Intent]
    K --> G
```

***

## Payment Intent Status Handling

Both patterns need to map [Payment Intent statuses](/developer/checkout/overview#payment-intent-lifecycle) to user-facing actions.

The critical distinction:

* **`requires_payment`** — No funds received yet. The user can resume or **cancel** the Payment Intent.
* **`processing`** — Funds have been received (partial or full). The payment **cannot be canceled or refunded** at this point. The user can only wait for settlement to complete or continue paying the remaining balance.

```typescript theme={null}
function resolveAction(paymentIntent: PaymentIntent) {
  switch (paymentIntent.status) {
    case "requires_payment":
      return {
        action: "resume",
        clientSecret: paymentIntent.client_secret,
        label: "Payment started",
        cta: "Resume",
        canCancel: true,
      }

    case "processing":
      return {
        action: "wait",
        label: "Processing",
        cta: "Refresh status",
        canCancel: false,
      }

    case "succeeded":
      return {
        action: "fulfill",
        label: "Paid",
        cta: null,
        canCancel: false,
      }

    case "canceled":
      return {
        action: "restart",
        label: "Canceled",
        cta: "Buy again",
        canCancel: false,
      }
  }
}
```

| Status             | User Label      | CTA                | Cancellable         | Behavior                                                 |
| ------------------ | --------------- | ------------------ | ------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `requires_payment` | Payment started | **Resume**         | Yes                 | Call `beginCheckout()` with same `client_secret`         |
| `processing`       | Processing      | **Refresh status** | No — funds received | Re-fetch status. Do **not** create a new Payment Intent. |
| `succeeded`        | Paid            | —                  | No                  | Fulfill credits.                                         |
| `canceled`         | Canceled        | **Buy again**      | —                   | Create a new Payment Intent.                             |

<Warning>
  Once a Payment Intent moves to `processing`, funds have been received on-chain. The payment cannot be canceled or refunded through the Unifold API. Never create a new Payment Intent while the current one is `processing` — this risks charging the user twice.
</Warning>

***

## Partial Payments

Unifold Payment Intents track partial payments natively via `amount_received`. When a user has paid some but not all of the amount, the Payment Intent moves to `processing` status. Once in `processing`, funds have been received on-chain — the Payment Intent cannot be canceled or refunded.

```typescript theme={null}
interface PaymentIntent {
  amount: string           // "9990000" ($9.99)
  amount_received: string  // "5000000" ($5.00)
  status: string           // "processing"
}
```

Both patterns should display partial progress:

```text theme={null}
11,000 Credits ($9.99)
Paid: $5.00  ·  Remaining: $4.99
[Continue payment]
```

When the user clicks "Continue payment," you resume the same Payment Intent. The checkout modal picks up from the partial state automatically — you do not need to create a new Payment Intent for the remaining balance.

<Note>
  You do not need to create a new Payment Intent for the remaining balance. Unifold tracks partial settlements on the existing Payment Intent. Just resume with the same `client_secret`.
</Note>

***

## User-Facing States

Regardless of which pattern you choose, map Payment Intent state to clear, non-technical labels:

### Labels and CTAs

| State                                 | Label                 | CTA                  | Cancel allowed       |
| ------------------------------------- | --------------------- | -------------------- | -------------------- |
| No incomplete Payment Intent          | Buy {credits} Credits | **Buy Now**          | —                    |
| `requires_payment`                    | Payment not complete  | **Continue payment** | Yes                  |
| `processing`, partial amount received | Partially paid        | **Continue payment** | No — funds received  |
| `processing`, no amount received yet  | Payment processing    | **Refresh status**   | No — funds in flight |
| `succeeded`                           | Purchased             | —                    | No                   |
| `canceled`                            | Canceled              | **Start again**      | —                    |

***

## The Complete Flow

```mermaid theme={null}
sequenceDiagram
    participant User
    participant Frontend
    participant Backend
    participant Unifold as Unifold API

    User->>Frontend: Opens credit store
    Frontend->>Backend: GET /packs (authenticated)
    Backend->>Unifold: List Payment Intents (external_user_id + status)
    Unifold-->>Backend: Processing Payment Intents
    Backend->>Backend: Match to packs via metadata
    Backend-->>Frontend: Packs + pending state per pack

    Frontend->>Frontend: Render pack grid (with pending indicators)

    alt User clicks Buy Now / Continue
        Frontend->>Backend: POST /purchase (packId)
        Backend->>Unifold: List Payment Intents (check for existing)
        
        alt Existing Payment Intent for this pack
            Unifold-->>Backend: Existing Payment Intent
            Backend-->>Frontend: { action: resume, clientSecret }
        else No existing Payment Intent
            Backend->>Unifold: Create Payment Intent
            Unifold-->>Backend: New Payment Intent with client_secret
            Backend-->>Frontend: { action: checkout, clientSecret }
        end
        
        Frontend->>Frontend: beginCheckout({ clientSecret })
    end

    User->>Frontend: Completes payment
    Unifold-->>Backend: Webhook: payment_intent.succeeded
    Backend->>Backend: Credit user account with pack credits
```

***

## Implementation Checklist

<Steps>
  <Step title="Choose your pattern">
    **Pattern A** if the pack grid is the primary purchase surface and you want invisible resume behind "Buy Now." **Pattern B** if you want an explicit pending payments section, or already have a billing/account page. **Both** for the best experience.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Store pack info in Payment Intent metadata">
    Always pass `metadata: { pack_id, credits }` and a `description` when [creating Payment Intents](/api-reference/payment-intents/create). This lets you render meaningful labels when listing Payment Intents later.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Guard against duplicate Payment Intents">
    Before creating a new Payment Intent, [list existing Payment Intents](/api-reference/payment-intents/list) filtered by `external_user_id` + `status` and match against `metadata`, `description`, or whichever field you use to identify packs. Both patterns use this same approach.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Handle webhooks as source of truth">
    Listen for [`payment_intent.processing`](/developer/webhooks/events/payment-intent#payment_intentprocessing) and [`payment_intent.succeeded`](/developer/webhooks/events/payment-intent#payment_intentsucceeded). Credit the user's account on `succeeded` — not on frontend `onSuccess`.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Clean up stale intents">
    Periodically [cancel](/api-reference/payment-intents/cancel) Payment Intents that have been in `requires_payment` for too long so they don't accumulate.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Disable Buy Now while processing">
    If the user has a Payment Intent in `processing` for a given pack, disable the "Buy Now" button for that pack or show the processing state instead.
  </Step>
</Steps>

***

## Pattern Comparison

|                            | Pattern A: Inline Resume                | Pattern B: Pending List                            |
| -------------------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- |
| **Prevents duplicates**    | Check-before-create on click            | Same check-before-create on click                  |
| **Where user resumes**     | Same pack card they'd normally buy from | Separate pending payments section                  |
| **Resume discoverability** | High — user sees it on the pack grid    | Lower — user must look at the pending section      |
| **User experience**        | Invisible resume — "Buy Now" just works | Explicit list — user picks which payment to resume |
| **Multiple pending packs** | Each pack card reflects its own state   | All pending Payment Intents listed in one place    |
| **Best for**               | Pack grid is the main purchase surface  | Apps with an existing account/billing page         |

***

## Rules of Thumb

| Do                                                                                  | Don't                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Check for existing pending Payment Intents before creating a new one                | Create a new Payment Intent every time the user clicks "Buy Now"        |
| Resume with the same `client_secret` when status is `requires_payment`              | Create a replacement when the old one is still usable                   |
| Use `metadata` or `description` to tie each Payment Intent to a pack                | Rely on amount alone to identify which pack a Payment Intent belongs to |
| Use [webhooks](/developer/webhooks/overview) to credit accounts                     | Fulfill based solely on frontend `onSuccess` callbacks                  |
| Show user-friendly labels for payment states                                        | Expose raw status strings like `requires_payment` directly in the UI    |
| [Cancel stale Payment Intents](/api-reference/payment-intents/cancel) on a schedule | Let orphaned Payment Intents linger indefinitely                        |

***

# Build a Themeable Headless Deposit Flow

> Wire the headless SDK into one reusable deposit hook, then skin it with any number of fully custom themes — the exact pattern behind the headless demo.

The headless SDK gives you the deposit **engine** (address creation, detection, auto-swap, settlement) with **none of the UI**. That split lets you do something the modal can't: keep all of your deposit logic in one place and render it a dozen different ways.

This recipe builds a complete deposit flow end to end and then re-skins it across multiple **themes** — a minimalist screen, an iOS sheet, and as many more as you want — all driven by a single shared hook.

<Info>
  New to the session-vs-execution model or the `useDeposit` API surface? Skim the [headless overview](/get-started/sdk-reference/react/headless/overview) and the [`useDeposit` reference](/get-started/sdk-reference/react/headless/use-deposit) first. This recipe assumes that vocabulary and focuses on the end-to-end architecture.
</Info>

***

## Build it, step by step

<Steps>
  <Step title="Install and wrap your app in the provider">
    The headless hooks ship inside `@unifold/connect-react`. Import the provider from the `/headless` subpath so a pure-headless app never pulls the modal/card UI into its bundle.

    <CodeGroup>
      ```bash npm theme={null}
      npm install @unifold/connect-react
      ```

      ```bash pnpm theme={null}
      pnpm add @unifold/connect-react
      ```
    </CodeGroup>

    ```tsx app/providers.tsx theme={null}
    "use client";

    import type { ReactNode } from "react";
    import { UnifoldProvider } from "@unifold/connect-react/headless";

    import { PUBLISHABLE_KEY } from "@/lib/unifold";

    export function Providers({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
      return (
        <UnifoldProvider publishableKey={PUBLISHABLE_KEY}>
          {children}
        </UnifoldProvider>
      );
    }
    ```

    ```tsx app/layout.tsx theme={null}
    import { Providers } from "./providers";
    import "./globals.css";

    export default function RootLayout({ children }: { children: React.ReactNode }) {
      return (
        <html lang="en">
          <body>
            <Providers>{children}</Providers>
          </body>
        </html>
      );
    }
    ```

    <Note>
      If you also use the modal SDK, import `UnifoldProvider` from `@unifold/connect-react` instead and keep a single provider so both surfaces share one `QueryClient` and cache.
    </Note>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Centralize your config in one module">
    Everything the flow needs — where funds settle, the user id, confirmation mode, and a few UI helpers — lives in one file. Keeping the **destination** as a module-level constant matters: changing any destination field replaces the session (and its address), so an inline object that changes identity every render would churn the session.

    ```tsx lib/unifold.ts theme={null}
    import type { ChainType, DirectExecution } from "@unifold/connect-react/headless";

    // Where the demo settles funds. In a real app this is your treasury target:
    // the chain + token you want to hold, and the address that receives it.
    export const DESTINATION = {
      chainType: "ethereum" as ChainType,
      chainId: "8453", // Base
      tokenAddress: "0x833589fCD6eDb6E08f4c7C32D4f71b54bdA02913", // USDC on Base
      recipientAddress:
        process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_UNIFOLD_RECIPIENT_ADDRESS ?? "0xYourTreasury",
    };

    export const DESTINATION_LABEL = "USDC on Base";

    // Your platform's stable, signed-in user id. Providing it up front (plus
    // autoStart) means the deposit begins on mount with no button press.
    export const DEMO_EXTERNAL_USER_ID = "user_123";

    // 'auto' arms backend scanning a few seconds in; 'manual' waits for an
    // "I've sent it" button wired to confirmFundsSent().
    export const CONFIRMATION_MODE: "auto" | "manual" = "auto";

    export const PUBLISHABLE_KEY =
      process.env.NEXT_PUBLIC_UNIFOLD_PUBLISHABLE_KEY ?? "";
    ```

    A deposit's **outcome** lives on the execution, not the session status (which is lifecycle-only: `idle | creating_addresses | ready | processing | error`). Add two tiny helpers so every theme reads success/failure the same way:

    ```tsx lib/unifold.ts theme={null}
    // Compared as strings so this module — imported by a Server Component —
    // never needs a runtime import of the ExecutionStatus enum, which would
    // pull the client-only provider/React context into the RSC graph.
    export function isExecutionSucceeded(
      execution: DirectExecution | null | undefined,
    ): boolean {
      return execution?.status === "succeeded";
    }

    export function isExecutionFailed(
      execution: DirectExecution | null | undefined,
    ): boolean {
      const status = execution?.status;
      return status === "failed" || status === "refunded";
    }

    // Label + tone for a status badge: outcome (from the execution) wins,
    // otherwise map the lifecycle status.
    export function statusPresentation(
      status: string,
      execution?: DirectExecution | null,
    ): { label: string; tone: "neutral" | "progress" | "success" | "error" } {
      if (isExecutionSucceeded(execution)) return { label: "Succeeded", tone: "success" };
      if (isExecutionFailed(execution)) return { label: "Failed", tone: "error" };
      switch (status) {
        case "idle": return { label: "Initializing", tone: "neutral" };
        case "creating_addresses": return { label: "Preparing", tone: "neutral" };
        case "ready": return { label: "Awaiting funds", tone: "progress" };
        case "processing": return { label: "Processing", tone: "progress" };
        case "error": return { label: "Error", tone: "error" };
        default: return { label: status, tone: "neutral" };
      }
    }
    ```

    <Warning>
      If a Server Component imports this module (for example a Next.js `page.tsx` that reads `PUBLISHABLE_KEY`), keep it free of **runtime** imports from the SDK. `import type { … }` is erased at build time; `import { ExecutionStatus }` is not and drags the client-only provider into the server graph, crashing the render. That's why the helpers above compare status strings instead of importing the enum.
    </Warning>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Put all the logic in one hook">
    This is the heart of the pattern. `useDepositFlow` runs the session, exposes the source token/chain pickers, and derives a single `phase` your UI can switch on. Every theme calls it and renders the result.

    ```tsx hooks/useDepositFlow.ts theme={null}
    "use client";

    import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
    import {
      useDeposit,
      useSupportedDepositTokens,
      type ChainType,
    } from "@unifold/connect-react/headless";

    import {
      CONFIRMATION_MODE,
      DEMO_EXTERNAL_USER_ID,
      DESTINATION,
      DESTINATION_LABEL,
      isExecutionFailed,
      isExecutionSucceeded,
      statusPresentation,
    } from "@/lib/unifold";

    export type DepositPhase = "live" | "detected" | "check" | "summary";

    export function useDepositFlow() {
      // 1. The deposit session. externalUserId is present from first render +
      //    autoStart, so it begins on mount with no button press.
      const deposit = useDeposit({
        externalUserId: DEMO_EXTERNAL_USER_ID,
        destination: DESTINATION,
        autoStart: true,
        confirmationMode: CONFIRMATION_MODE,
      });

      // 2. Source tokens/chains the user can deposit FROM (with per-chain
      //    minimums), straight from the endpoint — powers the two pickers.
      const tokens = useSupportedDepositTokens({ destination: DESTINATION }).data ?? [];

      const [selectedSymbol, setSelectedSymbol] = useState<string>();
      const [selectedChainKey, setSelectedChainKey] = useState<string>();
      const chainKey = (c: { chain_type: string; chain_id: string }) =>
        `${c.chain_type}:${c.chain_id}`;

      const token = tokens.find((t) => t.symbol === selectedSymbol) ?? tokens[0];
      const chains = token?.chains ?? [];
      const chain = chains.find((c) => chainKey(c) === selectedChainKey) ?? chains[0];

      // The real deposit address for the selected source chain.
      const address = chain
        ? deposit.getAddress({ chainType: chain.chain_type as ChainType })?.address
        : undefined;

      // 3. Outcome lives on the execution, not the session status — but
      //    latestExecution *persists* after a deposit settles. A second
      //    deposit in the same session would therefore start out reading the
      //    previous execution's "succeeded", fast-forwarding the phase machine
      //    past the QR. Track the execution we've already retired and only
      //    treat an outcome as current when it comes from a NEW one.
      const executionId = deposit.latestExecution?.id;
      const [retiredExecutionId, setRetiredExecutionId] = useState<
        string | undefined
      >(executionId);
      const isCurrentExecution =
        !!executionId && executionId !== retiredExecutionId;

      const succeeded =
        isCurrentExecution && isExecutionSucceeded(deposit.latestExecution);
      const failed =
        isCurrentExecution && isExecutionFailed(deposit.latestExecution);

      // 4. View phase machine: live → detected → check → summary, with short
      //    minimum display times so each beat is visible even when the backend
      //    settles almost instantly.
      const detected = deposit.status === "processing" || succeeded;
      const [phase, setPhase] = useState<DepositPhase>("live");
      const sourceKey = chain
        ? `${token?.symbol}:${chainKey(chain)}`
        : token?.symbol;

      // New token/chain → reset the view AND retire the settled execution, so
      // its stale "succeeded" can't push the fresh attempt off "live" (which
      // is the only phase that renders the QR).
      useEffect(() => {
        setPhase("live");
        setRetiredExecutionId(executionId);
      }, [sourceKey]);
      useEffect(() => {
        if (detected && phase === "live") setPhase("detected");
      }, [detected, phase]);
      useEffect(() => {
        if (phase !== "detected" || !succeeded) return;
        const t = setTimeout(() => setPhase("check"), 2500);
        return () => clearTimeout(t);
      }, [phase, succeeded]);
      useEffect(() => {
        if (phase !== "check") return;
        const t = setTimeout(() => setPhase("summary"), 2200);
        return () => clearTimeout(t);
      }, [phase]);
      useEffect(() => {
        if (failed) setPhase("live"); // resend from the QR
      }, [failed]);

      // Only surface an execution outcome in the badge when it belongs to the
      // current attempt. latestExecution persists after settling, so passing it
      // unconditionally would show a stale "Succeeded"/"Failed" even after the
      // flow reset to "live" (QR showing) for a new deposit.
      const { label: statusLabel, tone: statusTone } = statusPresentation(
        deposit.status,
        isCurrentExecution ? deposit.latestExecution : null,
      );

      return {
        // picker options (icons + per-chain minimums)
        tokenOptions: tokens.map((t) => ({ value: t.symbol, label: t.symbol })),
        chainOptions: chains.map((c) => ({
          value: chainKey(c),
          label: c.chain_name,
          right: `$${c.minimum_deposit_amount_usd.toFixed(2)}`,
        })),
        // data the UI renders
        address,
        option: chain && { minUsd: chain.minimum_deposit_amount_usd },
        execution: deposit.latestExecution,
        destinationLabel: DESTINATION_LABEL,
        // status + phase
        status: deposit.status,
        statusLabel,
        statusTone,
        phase,
        error: deposit.error,
        retry: deposit.start,
        confirmFundsSent: deposit.confirmFundsSent,
        isCheckingDeposit: deposit.isCheckingDeposit,
        // selection
        selectedSymbol: token?.symbol,
        selectedChainKey: chain ? chainKey(chain) : undefined,
        selectToken: (symbol: string) => {
          setSelectedSymbol(symbol);
          setSelectedChainKey(undefined);
        },
        selectChain: setSelectedChainKey,
      };
    }

    /** "$1,234.56" from the SDK's raw USD strings. */
    export function formatUsd(v: string | null | undefined) {
      const n = Number(v);
      return v && Number.isFinite(n) ? n.toFixed(2) : undefined;
    }
    ```

    <Tip>
      The `phase` machine is a UX nicety, not a requirement — settlement can be near-instant, and stepping through *detected → check → summary* with small timeouts keeps the animation legible. If you don't need that, render straight off `deposit.status` and `latestExecution?.status`.
    </Tip>

    <Warning>
      `latestExecution` sticks around after a deposit settles, so any outcome you derive from it (`succeeded` / `failed`) stays `true` into the *next* deposit unless you retire it. Without the `retiredExecutionId` guard above, starting a second deposit in the same session resets `phase` to `"live"` and then immediately snaps it back to `"detected"` (because `succeeded` is still `true`), and the QR never renders. Gate execution-derived outcomes on a fresh execution `id` whenever a session can host more than one deposit.
    </Warning>
  </Step>

  <Step title="Render a screen from the hook">
    A theme is now trivial: call the hook, branch on `phase` / `status`, and render your own markup. Here's a compact one using CSS Modules.

    ```tsx app/themes/minimal/page.tsx theme={null}
    "use client";

    import { DotQRCode } from "@/components/DotQRCode";
    import { Picker } from "@/components/Picker";
    import { useDepositFlow, formatUsd } from "@/hooks/useDepositFlow";
    import s from "./minimal.module.css";

    export default function MinimalTheme() {
      const f = useDepositFlow();

      return (
        <div className={s.wrap}>
          <div className={s.top}>
            <span className={s.kicker}>Deposit</span>
            <span className={s.status}>{f.statusLabel.toLowerCase()}</span>
          </div>

          {/* Same two pickers every theme uses. */}
          <div className={s.route}>
            <Picker value={f.selectedSymbol} options={f.tokenOptions} onChange={f.selectToken} ariaLabel="Token" />
            <Picker value={f.selectedChainKey} options={f.chainOptions} onChange={f.selectChain} ariaLabel="Network" />
          </div>
          <p className={s.dest}>→ {f.destinationLabel}</p>

          <div className={s.body}>
            {f.status === "error" ? (
              <button onClick={f.retry}>retry → {f.error?.message}</button>
            ) : f.phase === "summary" ? (
              <p className={s.big}>${formatUsd(f.execution?.destinationAmountUsd) ?? "—"} received</p>
            ) : f.phase === "check" ? (
              <p className={s.big}>Complete.</p>
            ) : f.phase === "detected" ? (
              <p className={s.big}>Detected…</p>
            ) : f.address ? (
              <div className={s.qrRow}>
                <DotQRCode value={f.address} size={150} clearCenter={0.26} />
                <button onClick={() => navigator.clipboard?.writeText(f.address!)}>
                  {f.address.slice(0, 8)}…{f.address.slice(-6)}
                </button>
              </div>
            ) : (
              <p className={s.big}>Preparing…</p>
            )}
          </div>
        </div>
      );
    }
    ```

    That is a complete, fully custom deposit screen. Every other theme is the same shape with different markup and CSS.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Make shared widgets themeable">
    The one interactive widget every theme reuses is the source-token/chain picker. Keep it presentational and let it read its colors and typography from CSS variables the surrounding theme sets, so it adopts each look automatically.

    ```tsx components/Picker.tsx theme={null}
    "use client";

    import { useState } from "react";
    import pk from "./picker.module.css";

    export interface PickerOption {
      value: string;
      label: string;
      icon?: string;
      right?: string; // e.g. a per-chain minimum
    }

    export function Picker({
      value,
      options,
      onChange,
      ariaLabel,
    }: {
      value: string | undefined;
      options: PickerOption[];
      onChange: (value: string) => void;
      ariaLabel?: string;
    }) {
      const [open, setOpen] = useState(false);
      const selected = options.find((o) => o.value === value) ?? options[0];

      return (
        <div className={pk.picker}>
          <button className={pk.trigger} onClick={() => setOpen((o) => !o)} aria-label={ariaLabel}>
            <span>{selected?.label ?? "Select"}</span>
            <span data-open={open}>▾</span>
          </button>
          {open && (
            <div className={pk.menu} role="listbox">
              {options.map((o) => (
                <button key={o.value} className={pk.option} onClick={() => { onChange(o.value); setOpen(false); }}>
                  <span>{o.label}</span>
                  {o.right && <span className={pk.oRight}>{o.right}</span>}
                </button>
              ))}
            </div>
          )}
        </div>
      );
    }
    ```

    ```css components/picker.module.css theme={null}
    /* Each theme sets --pk-bg / --pk-fg / --pk-radius on a parent, and the
       picker inherits them — no per-theme copy of this component needed. */
    .trigger {
      background: var(--pk-bg, #fff);
      color: var(--pk-fg, #111);
      border-radius: var(--pk-radius, 10px);
    }
    ```
  </Step>

  <Step title="Add as many themes as you like">
    A new theme is a new route with its own CSS Module — zero new logic. Because they all call `useDepositFlow()`, they stay behavior-identical and only diverge visually.

    <Tabs>
      <Tab title="iOS Sheet">
        ```tsx app/themes/ios/page.tsx theme={null}
        "use client";
        import { useDepositFlow } from "@/hooks/useDepositFlow";
        import s from "./ios.module.css";

        export default function IosTheme() {
          const f = useDepositFlow();
          return (
            <div className={s.sheet}>
              <div className={s.titleRow}>
                <h1>Add Funds</h1>
                <span data-tone={f.statusTone}>{f.statusLabel}</span>
              </div>
              {/* pickers + phase branches, styled as a native bottom sheet */}
            </div>
          );
        }
        ```
      </Tab>

      <Tab title="Theme gallery">
        ```tsx app/themes/page.tsx theme={null}
        import Link from "next/link";

        const THEMES = [
          { slug: "minimal", name: "Minimalist" },
          { slug: "ios", name: "iOS Sheet" },
          { slug: "cyber", name: "Cyberpunk" },
          // …add a slug per theme route
        ];

        export default function ThemesIndex() {
          return (
            <div className="theme-grid">
              {THEMES.map((t) => (
                <Link key={t.slug} href={`/themes/${t.slug}`}>{t.name}</Link>
              ))}
            </div>
          );
        }
        ```
      </Tab>
    </Tabs>

    <Note>
      Every theme shares the same `useDepositFlow()` instance semantics: it starts its own session on mount and tears it down on unmount. Navigating between theme routes starts a fresh session each time — expected for a gallery, and exactly how a real single-screen deposit page behaves.
    </Note>
  </Step>
</Steps>

***

## One hook, any layout: single screen or wizard

Themes change how the flow *looks*; the same decoupling lets you change how it's *shaped*. Because `useDepositFlow()` owns all the state, the presentation layer is free to render everything on one screen **or** split it across guided steps — without touching the deposit logic.

That's a real UX lever, because deposit audiences differ:

<CardGroup cols={2}>
  <Card title="Crypto natives" icon="bolt">
    Show everything at once: token + network pickers, the address/QR, and the minimum on a single dense screen. They know what to send and just want the address fast.
  </Card>

  <Card title="Newcomers" icon="hand">
    Walk them through it: **pick a token → pick a network → send to this address → confirming → done**. One decision per screen, with copy that explains each step.
  </Card>
</CardGroup>

A wizard is just a local step index layered over the same hook — you read the hook's values on each step and advance with your own buttons:

```tsx app/themes/wizard/page.tsx theme={null}
"use client";

import { useState } from "react";
import { DotQRCode } from "@/components/DotQRCode";
import { Picker } from "@/components/Picker";
import { useDepositFlow } from "@/hooks/useDepositFlow";

type Step = "token" | "network" | "send";

export default function WizardTheme() {
  const f = useDepositFlow();
  const [step, setStep] = useState<Step>("token");

  // The SDK still drives the outcome: once funds are detected/settled, jump
  // straight to the flow's own phase UI, no matter which step the user is on.
  if (f.phase !== "live") return <DepositProgress phase={f.phase} execution={f.execution} />;

  return (
    <div className="wizard">
      {step === "token" && (
        <Panel title="1 · What are you sending?" hint="Pick the coin you already hold.">
          <Picker value={f.selectedSymbol} options={f.tokenOptions} onChange={f.selectToken} ariaLabel="Token" />
          <button onClick={() => setStep("network")}>Continue</button>
        </Panel>
      )}

      {step === "network" && (
        <Panel title="2 · Which network?" hint="Choose the chain you'll send from.">
          <Picker value={f.selectedChainKey} options={f.chainOptions} onChange={f.selectChain} ariaLabel="Network" />
          <button onClick={() => setStep("token")}>Back</button>
          <button onClick={() => setStep("send")} disabled={!f.address}>Continue</button>
        </Panel>
      )}

      {step === "send" && f.address && (
        <Panel title="3 · Send your deposit" hint={`Minimum $${f.option?.minUsd.toFixed(2)}. Settles as ${f.destinationLabel}.`}>
          <DotQRCode value={f.address} size={180} clearCenter={0.28} />
          <button onClick={() => navigator.clipboard?.writeText(f.address!)}>Copy address</button>
          <button onClick={() => setStep("network")}>Back</button>
        </Panel>
      )}
    </div>
  );
}
```

<Note>
  Let the **user** drive the early steps (token → network → send), but let the **SDK** drive the rest. Detection and settlement can happen the moment funds arrive, so branch on `f.phase` (or `deposit.status` / `latestExecution`) *before* your step switch — otherwise a deposit that lands while the user is still on step 2 would go unnoticed. The example above short-circuits to the progress UI as soon as `phase` leaves `"live"`.
</Note>

<Tip>
  You don't have to choose one forever. Ship the wizard as its own route (`/themes/wizard`) alongside the single-screen themes and pick per surface — a guided flow in onboarding, the compact screen in a power-user settings page — all backed by the one `useDepositFlow()` hook.
</Tip>

***

## Manual confirmation (optional)

Set `CONFIRMATION_MODE = 'manual'` to require an explicit "I've sent it" step. The button prompts the backend to scan, and `isCheckingDeposit` reflects that it's running. Because it's part of the session, any theme can render it off the hook:

```tsx theme={null}
{f.status === "ready" && CONFIRMATION_MODE === "manual" && (
  <button onClick={f.confirmFundsSent} disabled={f.isCheckingDeposit}>
    {f.isCheckingDeposit ? "Checking…" : "I've sent the transfer"}
  </button>
)}
```

`useDepositFlow` already forwards `confirmFundsSent` and `isCheckingDeposit` from `useDeposit`, so any theme can render this button.

***

## Credit balances on your backend, not the client

The client-side outcome (`latestExecution.status === 'succeeded'`) is perfect for updating the UI, but it is **not** where you credit balances — a browser can close mid-flight. Treat the client as presentation and let your server be the source of truth via [webhooks](/developer/webhooks/events/deposit).

The execution `id` is your deduplication key, and the `external_user_id` you passed to `useDeposit` comes back in the webhook for attribution.

<Warning>
  Never credit a user's balance solely from client state. Confirm the settled execution server-side, deduplicate on the execution `id`, then write to your ledger. The [Deposit as Stablecoin recipe](/recipes/treasury/deposit-as-stablecoin) covers the full backend pattern.
</Warning>

***

## Recap

| You write once                                         | You write per theme                                |
| ------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- |
| `useDepositFlow()` — session, selection, phase machine | A component that reads the hook and renders markup |
| `lib/unifold.ts` — destination, config, status helpers | A CSS Module for the look                          |
| Shared widgets (`Picker`, QR) driven by CSS variables  | Which widgets to place, and where                  |

**The one thing to remember:** headless means logic and presentation are fully separated. Put every deposit behavior in one hook; make each theme a thin presentational layer over it. Ship one look or twelve — the engine underneath never changes.

# Points Balance Platform: Deposit as Stablecoin

> Learn how to build a reliable deposit flow that converts any crypto deposit into USDC-backed user balances

## What is a Points Balance Platform?

A **points balance platform** is any application that maintains a credit balance for users on your platform—points, rewards, credits, cashback, referral bonuses, or any internal currency. Users can acquire this balance through actions (purchases, engagement, referrals) or by **depositing real value**.

This recipe focuses on the **deposit-as-stablecoin** flow: allowing users to fund their platform balance by sending **any cryptocurrency from any chain**, which Unifold automatically converts to USDC in your treasury.

<Info>
  Unifold handles the complexity of multi-chain deposits and token swaps. Users can deposit ETH, SOL, POL, or any supported token—Unifold converts it to USDC on your chosen chain, and you credit their balance in points.
</Info>

Rather than prescriptive code, we'll focus on **principles you can adapt** to your own stack and requirements.

***

## Shared Concept: The Points Balance System

Both deposits and withdrawals operate on the same fundamental abstraction: **a platform-managed balance that represents value**, with Unifold handling the blockchain complexity on both ends.

```mermaid theme={null}
flowchart LR
    subgraph External["User's Crypto"]
        A[Any Token]
        B[Any Chain]
    end
    
    subgraph Unifold["Unifold Layer"]
        C[Deposit Address]
        D[Auto-Swap]
        E[Outbound API]
    end
    
    subgraph Platform["Your Platform"]
        F[Treasury USDC]
        G[Points Ledger]
        H[User Balance]
    end
    
    A -->|deposit| C
    B --> C
    C --> D
    D -->|USDC| F
    F -->|webhook| G
    G -->|credit| H
    H -->|withdrawal| G
    G -->|debit| E
    E -->|USDC| A
```

**Why use an internal balance instead of on-chain tokens?**

| Benefit                     | Explanation                                                                      |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| **Instant transactions**    | Internal balance updates are database writes—milliseconds, not block times       |
| **Zero gas fees for users** | Users interact with your platform, not the blockchain directly                   |
| **Flexible business logic** | Apply bonuses, tiers, expiration, or custom rules without smart contract changes |
| **Better UX**               | Users don't need wallets or crypto knowledge to earn and use points              |
| **Unified accounting**      | One ledger tracks all value movements regardless of source                       |
| **Multi-chain abstraction** | Accept deposits from any chain, withdraw to any chain—your ledger stays simple   |

<Note>
  The internal balance acts as a **bridge** between blockchain value and platform functionality. Unifold converts any incoming crypto to USDC (deposits) and sends USDC out to any destination (withdrawals). Your platform just manages the points ledger.
</Note>

***

## The Flow of Funds: Any Crypto to Balance

When a user deposits cryptocurrency, the value flows through Unifold's auto-swap layer before landing as USDC in your treasury:

```mermaid theme={null}
sequenceDiagram
    participant User as User Wallet
    participant Unifold as Unifold SDK
    participant Deposit as Deposit Address
    participant Swap as Auto-Swap
    participant Treasury as Treasury (USDC)
    participant Backend as Your Backend
    participant Ledger as Points Ledger
    
    User->>Unifold: Initiate deposit (any token)
    Unifold->>Deposit: Generate user's deposit address
    User->>Deposit: Send ETH/SOL/POL/etc.
    Deposit->>Swap: Auto-swap to USDC
    Swap->>Treasury: USDC delivered
    Treasury->>Backend: Webhook: deposit complete
    Backend->>Ledger: Credit user balance
    Backend->>User: Notify deposit complete
```

**What Unifold handles for you:**

| Concern                   | Without Unifold                   | With Unifold                           |
| ------------------------- | --------------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| **Multi-chain support**   | Build indexers for each chain     | Accept deposits from 10+ chains        |
| **Token variety**         | Only accept USDC                  | Accept any token, auto-convert to USDC |
| **User attribution**      | Manage deposit addresses yourself | Unique addresses per user, automatic   |
| **Swap execution**        | Integrate DEXs, handle slippage   | Automatic best-route swaps             |
| **Confirmation tracking** | Monitor each chain's finality     | Unified webhook when complete          |

<Steps>
  <Step title="User initiates deposit">
    Using the Unifold SDK, the user sees a deposit modal showing their unique deposit address. They can send any supported token from any chain.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Unifold detects and swaps">
    Unifold monitors the deposit address. When tokens arrive, it automatically swaps them to USDC using the best available route.
  </Step>

  <Step title="USDC lands in treasury">
    The converted USDC is sent to your treasury account on your chosen chain (Polygon or Base).
  </Step>

  <Step title="Webhook notifies your backend">
    Unifold sends a webhook with the deposit details—execution ID, user ID, amount, and transaction hash.
  </Step>

  <Step title="Credit the ledger">
    Your backend creates the deposit record and credits the user's points balance.
  </Step>
</Steps>

**The conversion:**

| Stage             | Form                            | Location                        |
| ----------------- | ------------------------------- | ------------------------------- |
| User sends        | Any token (ETH, SOL, POL, etc.) | User's wallet → Deposit address |
| Auto-swap         | Any token → USDC                | Unifold infrastructure          |
| Treasury receives | USDC                            | Your treasury account           |
| User sees         | Points/credits                  | Platform ledger                 |

<Tip>
  The USDC stays in your treasury account—it's the **backing** for the user's platform balance. When they eventually withdraw, the USDC flows back out from treasury to their wallet.
</Tip>

***

## Using Unifold SDK for Deposits

Unifold provides a drop-in React SDK that handles the entire deposit flow—wallet connection, address generation, deposit tracking, and completion notification.

### Installation

<CodeGroup>
  ```bash npm theme={null}
  npm install @unifold/connect-react
  ```

  ```bash pnpm theme={null}
  pnpm add @unifold/connect-react
  ```

  ```bash yarn theme={null}
  yarn add @unifold/connect-react
  ```
</CodeGroup>

### Setup the Provider

Wrap your app with `UnifoldProvider`:

```tsx theme={null}
import { UnifoldProvider } from '@unifold/connect-react';
import '@unifold/connect-react/styles.css';

function App() {
  return (
    <UnifoldProvider 
      publishableKey="pk_live_your_publishable_key"
      config={{
        modalTitle: 'Add Funds',
      }}
    >
      <YourApp />
    </UnifoldProvider>
  );
}
```

### Launch the Deposit Modal

When a user wants to add funds, call `beginDeposit()` with your treasury as the recipient:

```tsx theme={null}
import { useUnifold } from '@unifold/connect-react';

function AddFundsButton() {
  const { beginDeposit } = useUnifold();

  const handleAddFunds = async () => {
    try {
      const result = await beginDeposit({
        // Your internal user ID — used for attribution
        externalUserId: 'user_abc123',
        
        // Where the USDC should land (your treasury)
        destinationChainType: 'ethereum',
        destinationChainId: '137',  // Polygon
        destinationTokenAddress: '0x3c499c542cEF5E3811e1192ce70d8cC03d5c3359', // USDC
        destinationTokenSymbol: 'USDC',
        
        // Your treasury address
        recipientAddress: '0xYourTreasuryAddress',
      });
      
      // Deposit complete! The webhook will fire with details.
      console.log('Deposit completed:', result.executionId);
      
    } catch (error) {
      console.error('Deposit failed:', error);
    }
  };

  return (
    <button onClick={handleAddFunds}>
      Add Funds
    </button>
  );
}
```

<Note>
  The `externalUserId` parameter is critical—it's how Unifold attributes the deposit to the correct user. Use your internal user ID that you'll receive in the webhook.
</Note>

### What the User Sees

The Unifold modal provides a complete deposit experience:

1. **Deposit address** — A unique address for this user, with QR code
2. **Supported tokens** — Visual list of accepted tokens and chains
3. **Live tracking** — Real-time status as the deposit is detected, swapped, and confirmed
4. **Completion** — Success state with transaction details

The user can deposit from any wallet (MetaMask, Coinbase Wallet, hardware wallets, exchange withdrawals) without connecting it to your app.

### Supported Deposit Chains and Tokens

Users can deposit from any of these chains:

| Chain                                                                                                                                                                                               | Chain Type | Chain ID  | Example Tokens        |

| <img src="/_mintlify/image/unifold/images/chains/base.svg" alt="Base" style={{ width: '16px', height: '16px', display: 'inline', verticalAlign: 'middle', marginRight: '6px' }} /> Base             | `ethereum` | `8453`    | ETH, USDC             |
